title: Design a Batched LLM Inference Service
prompt:
Design a batched LLM inference service backed by a GPU fleet. The service should improve throughput while keeping latency predictable for client workloads ranging from a single input to a list of 100 inputs.

The core exercise uses a fixed-batch contract: a request becomes a durable job, the scheduler forms fixed batches, and GPU workers execute them. Do not use continuous batching or traffic rate limiting as the primary answer. State the SLOs and product assumptions you need before choosing the batch size and wait window.

Cover:

- API semantics for submission, idempotency, cancellation, status, and result retrieval.
- The durable write path, queueing model, fixed-batch scheduler, GPU-aware dispatch, and worker lifecycle.
- How your design balances throughput, queueing delay, fairness, model placement, and GPU utilization.
- Partial failures, retries, scaling the GPU fleet, observability, and capacity signals.
- How you would review a flawed design document for missing assumptions, queue/scheduler mismatch, weak backpressure, or unsafe retry behavior.

This is a practice reconstruction of a recurring Anthropic ML-systems design signal from the Opportunity 2026 question bank. It preserves the reported batch-inference and review-mode themes, but is not presented as a verbatim interview script or a confirmed interviewer rubric.

response.reference_answer:
## 1. Frame the contract before designing

I would first ask whether the client submits one prompt per request or a durable job containing up to 100 inputs, whether outputs may stream, whether requests share one model version, and which SLO matters: submission acknowledgement, time-to-first-token, or full-job completion. For this exercise I assume non-streaming batch jobs, one model version per job, durable results, and a fixed-batch scheduler. The design must make the batching wait visible in the latency budget.

## 2. API and state machine

POST /v1/batches accepts a model version, inputs, generation parameters, a client-provided idempotency key, and an optional priority class. It returns a batch_id after the request body and an Accepted state have been durably recorded. GET /v1/batches/{id} returns Accepted, Queued, Leased, Running, Succeeded, Failed, or Cancelled plus per-item status and result locations. DELETE /v1/batches/{id} is best effort: it cancels queued work immediately and records a cancellation request for a leased or running batch.

The idempotency key maps to the durable job record, so a timeout retry returns the original batch_id rather than creating new GPU work. Individual item IDs let a retry run only unfinished items after a partial worker failure.

## 3. Submission and fixed-batching path

An API tier validates model and payload limits, writes the job and item records to a durable store, and appends a queue record in the same transactional boundary or through an outbox. Queues are partitioned by compatible execution shape: model version, hardware class, and coarse input/output length bucket. The scheduler chooses the oldest eligible work fairly across priority classes, waits at most W milliseconds, and emits a batch once it reaches B compatible items or the wait expires. B and W are explicit control knobs: a larger B improves GPU efficiency but raises tail queueing delay.

This is intentionally not continuous batching. After dispatch, a fixed batch stays fixed for its GPU execution.

## 4. GPU fleet and placement

A GPU-aware dispatcher leases a batch to a healthy worker that already hosts the requested model replica when possible. Workers report model residency, free memory, executor occupancy, batch duration, and heartbeat health. Each worker owns a fixed-batch executor; a per-worker KV cache is optional optimization only when the workload has meaningful reuse and does not change the fixed-batch scheduling contract. A worker writes item results to durable result storage before marking the lease complete.

Scaling adds workers or replicas for the queue partitions with sustained age and utilization pressure. I would keep model placement separate from request scheduling: the placement controller decides which replicas should exist, while the dispatcher chooses among ready replicas.

## 5. Failure handling and backpressure

Leases expire and are reclaimed when a worker dies. Completion is idempotent, keyed by batch and item attempt IDs, so a late worker cannot overwrite a newer retry. The job record records completed items before any retry is released. Cancellation is checked before dispatch and at safe worker boundaries; a result that wins the race with cancellation is surfaced consistently as completed.

The service uses bounded durable queues and reports capacity exhaustion when it cannot safely accept more work. That is admission backpressure, not a traffic-rate policy. It protects accepted jobs from unbounded queueing delay.

## 6. Observability and review-mode critique

I would monitor accepted-to-complete latency split into queue wait and GPU execution, batch fill ratio, queue age by partition, worker utilization, model-load time, lease expirations, duplicate submissions, cancellation outcomes, and result-write failures. A capacity model should use measured per-shape execution time rather than average requests.

When reviewing a design document, I would flag missing SLOs, a global queue that mixes incompatible shapes, no durable idempotency boundary, a scheduler that waits forever for a full batch, GPU dispatch that ignores model residency, retry paths that duplicate completed work, and dashboards that hide queue wait behind one end-to-end latency number.

## 7. Main trade-off

I would start with small compatible queues, a fixed B, and a bounded W, then tune from observed queue wait and GPU occupancy. The correct operating point is workload-specific: forcing every batch to be full maximizes utilization only by spending too much latency, while dispatching every job immediately wastes GPU capacity. The design should make that trade-off measurable and reversible.
